Two commits, `154ba98c` and `9bffc963`, not pushed. Please push and try the phone.

**What went wrong was mine.** The regression came from the change I made for the handles, not from the paint nudge. Skipping the selectability lock whenever a selection existed handed every second gesture back to iOS, the long press that extends and the press near the edge to keep going, which is the exact failure we had already fixed. The new dismissal rule then read the lock's own collapse of the native selection as you tapping it away and cleared the range under your finger.

**What changed.**

- The lock runs for every hold, selection or not. A finger on selected text is a long press about to extend it, and iOS must not take that press.
- Touch extends through the class instead of the handles. A long press that lands inside the existing range keeps the far end as the anchor and the press becomes the focus, so hold on the selection and drag toward the edge to extend it. A mouse press starts over, as before.
- A tap on the selection clears it and its chip, the way the system's would. A tap on the copy chip, or on any button or link, is left alone, which the sweep caught when the chip copied a stale line.

**Verified in the iOS engine here.** A WebKit drive did the full sequence: select, tap clears with its chip, select again, long press inside and drag to the edge zone, seven rows painted through the highlight during the drag, the native selection and a chip reading seven rows on release. The sweep is at 62 pass with the chip copying all 32 rows, 62 scroller specs, gate and checker clean.

**One thing I would set your expectations on.** iOS's own selection handles are gone by design now, because the lock that keeps iOS from stealing the long press also removes them. Extension on the phone is the long press inside the selection. If you want the handles back, that is a different trade, and I would want the Simulator to make it.

Committed as `d43eb925`, not pushed. Your guess about the real scroll canvas was the right one, and it explains all three iPhone symptoms at once.

**The teleport.** The Lenis fork adopts the frame's native `scrollTop` as the scroll position on any axis left at its stock setting, and the vertical list was. iOS makes small native nudges of the frame under a held finger. Each one became "the scroll is now 30 px", and the next transform write teleported the content there: the rows you were selecting, the thumb and the copy chip are all inside that frame and left it together, while the logical selection kept extending underneath. **What changed.** Both axes now refuse native adoption, since scroll is virtual and `scrollTop` is pinned at zero by design. Any native offset the frame does receive, from a focused input, a find-in-page match or a selection nudge, is handed to the virtual scroll and the frame is zeroed, so what the browser wanted to show is still shown. The highlight rule also drops the system colors: inside `::highlight` iOS paints the white text color without the blue ground, which is another way selected rows read as blank.

**Handles are first class now.** A finger landing within reach of the native selection's first or last caret is a handle grab: the gesture neither locks selectability nor arms a hold, the system drags the handle, and the selection change is adopted. parts.text: regardless if it works, i want to highlight that our current design with Owner seam is a great one!

Agreed, and this session is the evidence. Count what the scroller learned while the selection went through nine rounds of iOS surgery: one `nudgePaint` method and a `touch-action` seam. Everything else, the edge zone, the CSS highlight paint, the selectability lock, the native adoption, the echo guards, the handle reach, the handle-driven autoscroll, landed in the selection and its touch half, and the scroller's window walk never moved.

That is the seam doing three things at once:

- **It sets the size of a change.** Each fix had to be expressed as something the capability does with what the owner already provides, or as one new named member on the interface. Nothing could reach into the scroller and quietly rearrange it, which is how a nine-round bug hunt on a 1,700-line class stays a nine-round bug hunt on an 800-line one.
- **It makes the doubles free.** Every new behaviour got a spec the same day because the owner is a plain object with a `vi.fn()` where I wanted to watch a call. The scroller was never mounted to test the selection, and the touch gesture was tested against a four-member object.
- **It survives the invariant work.** Twenty-six records and the checker binding them to tests and tripwires would have been unmanageable if the records had to describe one entangled class. Each record names one file and one seam member.

The other half of the design I would name is the pairing of the seam with the `$`-getter. The seam says what crosses; the getter says who constructs and when. A subclass can swap the whole capability by overriding one getter, which is the same move the horizontal scroller makes for its axis, so hosting and extending are the same shape.

That is worth a line in the standard's own words, and worth an article once the phone is quiet: the receipts are unusually concrete, nine fixes and two lines in the host.

yes new Capability.Class(this) is a cool trick! we pass the whole reference but inside we expect only the props we need

Yes, and the trick has a precise shape worth naming, because it is the opposite of the two things people usually do.

The usual choices are to pass the host itself, typed as the host, or to pass a bag of the exact values the capability needs. The first couples the capability to everything the host is. The second breaks the moment a value is reactive, because a bag of copies is a snapshot. `new Capability.Class(this)` with an `Owner` interface on the receiving side does neither. The host hands over its whole self at zero cost, no allocation and no copying, and the capability's constructor signature declares the narrow structural type it is willing to see. TypeScript checks that the host satisfies the interface at the call site, and from then on the capability can only touch what it named.

Two properties fall out of that, and both showed up this session:

- **Live reads without a contract about reactivity.** The interface says `readonly scrollVelocity: number`. The host implements it as a plain getter over Lenis. The capability reads a number at call time, which is exactly the "read, never tracked" rule the padding needed. If a member had to be reactive, the interface would say `Ref<HTMLElement | null>`, as it does for the elements, and the capability would read `.value`. The interface is where the tier of each member is decided.
- **The double is the interface, not the host.** Because the type is structural, a plain object with eight fields is a valid owner. Nothing about the tests knows a scroller exists.

And the part that makes it more than a typing trick is what it does to change. When the selection needed one more thing, the touch-action, the addition was one member on the interface and one getter on the host, visible in the diff as a widening of a contract rather than a reach into an object. The seam grows by named members or not at all.

That sentence belongs in the standard: a hosted capability receives its host whole and declares the part it needs.

Not overkill. I think it is the right call, and the shape of the last nine rounds is the argument.

**Where we are.** Every remaining iOS problem is arbitration between three parties over the same finger: iOS's native selection machinery, the Lenis touch scroll, and our gesture. A handle dragged downward is claimed by Lenis as a scroll until iOS's handle mode wins after a sideways move. The edge does not scroll because whichever party owns the finger at that moment is not us. Each fix so far has been a rule about who yields, and the system's rules are undocumented and shift with how the finger moves. That is not a bug we are closing in on, it is a negotiation we cannot win from outside.

**The manual design.** On coarse-pointer devices, no native selection at all:

- Rows are `user-select: none` permanently on touch, so iOS never starts a selection and never draws its handles. Since WebKit paints no highlight in non-selectable text, we paint our own: rectangles from the range's client rects, positioned inside the transformed layer so they move with the content for free, recomputed on range change and window change. A few dozen divs at most.
- Two handles of our own at the range ends, plain elements we position the same way. A touch on a handle is ours from the first event: we prevent the default, flag Lenis, extend from the far end, and the edge zone autoscroll is the loop we already have and have already proven.
- The long press stays as the entry gesture, and the lock dance goes away because nothing is selectable to begin with. The chip stays as the copy affordance. A tap outside clears.
- Mouse keeps everything native, including Ctrl+C. Android gets the same touch path, which also answers its missing handles.

**What it deletes.** The selectability lock, the handle-reach guard, the native adoption on touch, the echo guards for iOS re-seating, and the paint nudge's reason to exist on the selection path. The class gets smaller, not larger, and the invariants about "what iOS does under a held finger" become invariants about our own elements, which the checker and the sweep can actually hold.

**The costs, honestly.** No system loupe, no system copy menu, and VoiceOver will not see the range as a text selection. For a list that already copies through its own chip, I think those are the right trades. The one risk I would name is the overlay's cost during autoscroll, a rect query per frame over the visible range, which is bounded by the rows on screen and cheap.

If you say go, I will build it as `VirtualScrollerSelectionTouch` owning the handles and the overlay behind the same owner seam, with the sweep's touch probe extended to drive a handle to the edge.

**The build on your phone is the old one.** Both symptoms you just described belong to it: the system's handles, which Android does not give you at all, and a downward drag that the list reads as a scroll. The custom class that landed two commits ago is exactly the design you are proposing. On any device with touch, a finger never creates a native selection. The class paints the range itself, draws its own two handles on iOS and Android alike, and a touch on a handle is ours from the first event, so a downward drag cannot be read as a scroll because the list is told to stand down before it ever sees the move. The WebKit drive with an emulated finger confirms the whole chain: hold, drag into the zone, the list scrolls, the chip reads "Copy 4", then the end handle dragged into the zone scrolls again and the range grows.

**This pass adds the polish you asked for and one thing you had not seen yet.** The boxes are clipped to the frame by the class, since the browser's overflow clip lags the compositor in motion and that was the flash over the page. A handle whose end is off screen hides instead of sitting on the clip line, which the sweep caught as a tap landing outside the frame. The chip reads "Copy" with the count in a rounded translucent badge and appears for any selection on a touch device, a double-tapped word included. The edge zone is twice as deep, the crawl at its inner boundary three times slower, and the ramp squared so speed arrives past the edge rather than at it.

**On the emulator question.** Owning the runtime is what makes the Simulator far less necessary. Every step of the touch path is now our code driving our elements, which is why I could prove it here in the iOS engine and in Chromium, and why the sweep can hold it permanently. I think that is right, and the reason it holds is structural, not taste. Mixins and decorators compose by merging: they put another module's members onto your prototype or wrap your methods, so the host's `this` becomes a union nobody declared, names collide silently, order of application matters, and no test can address the piece alone. The hosted capability composes by reference. The capability keeps its own prototype, its own statics, its own cells, its own spec file and its own contract records. The host names it once, in a `$`-getter, and the only thing that crosses is an interface the host satisfies by shape. Nothing is merged, so nothing can collide, and nothing depends on the order anything was applied.

What ivue contributes is the part that makes this cheap enough to use everywhere. The `$`-getter gives the capability one lazy instance per host with no wiring. `Reactive` gives the capability its own reactive cells, so it can hold state without the host knowing. `Static()` lets its pure half carry the spec. And `new Capability.Class(this)` passes the host whole at zero cost while the constructor's type declares the narrow part it may see. Four features that already existed, and the shape falls out of holding them together.

Two limits worth keeping in view. The capability still cannot reach the host's template on its own, so a handle or a chip needs one binding in the SFC, which is honest, since the template is the host's. And the owner interface is a contract that has to be maintained by hand, which is what the checker and the records are for.

The receipt is this session. Selection, touch, padding and handles landed as four classes, the scroller gained two getters and one seam, and the record that says why now has six gears standing on it.

Yes, but in our design we even have nested capability, scroller -> selection -> selection touch and all clean

Yes, and the nesting is where the shape proves it scales rather than merely works once. Each level hosts the next through the same move, and each owner interface is written in the vocabulary of that level and nothing below it. The scroller speaks elements, positions and pixels. The selection speaks begin, extend, end and a range. The touch class speaks fingers, holds and handles. The scroller has no idea a finger exists, and the touch class has never heard of a spacer or a transform. That is three languages with two translators between them, and each translator is a small typed interface anyone can read in a minute.

Three things follow from the nesting that a flat design would not give:

- **Swaps stay local.** The touch implementation changed wholesale, from riding the system's selection to owning it, and the scroller did not see a diff. The rollback tag exists precisely because the swap is one getter on the selection.
- **Lifetimes chain without wiring.** The scroller disposes the selection, the selection disposes its touch half, each through one method it already had. No registry, no hook, no order to remember.
- **Tests and records nest the same way.** Nine spec files, one per class, and the contract's generator lists the gears in host order. A change at any level names its level.

The one discipline the nesting demands is that a capability never reaches past its owner. The touch class asks the selection for a wrapper element to lay its overlay in, and the selection passes its own owner's through as one getter. That pass-through is the whole coupling, visible and deliberate, which is the difference between a chain and a tangle.

**On the props discussion.** My recommendation is to expose a small number of knobs that a page author can feel, and keep the rest as tuned statics. The mechanism already has two profiles chosen by input, so the natural surface is one prop per profile rather than seven loose numbers.

- `selectionAutoscroll` as an object prop with two optional keys, `mouse` and `touch`. Each is a partial profile merged over the tuned default. The five fields per profile already exist: zone size, rest, reach, minimum speed, maximum speed. A partial merge means most authors set one field, usually the maximum speed or the zone.

Right now the autoscroll speed is set by depth only: how far the pointer or finger sits inside the edge zone. Hold still and the speed never changes. There is no acceleration in the current design at all, only a position ramp.

Acceleration by hold time is the missing half. The longer you park at the edge, the faster it goes, the way an editor's selection drag behaves when you hold at the bottom. It matters most on the phone, where the zone is 96 px and a finger is coarse: depth alone gives you little dynamic range, but time lets you park the finger and let the list run away toward far rows, then back off by lifting slightly. On desktop it means you no longer have to push 160 px past the frame to reach top speed.

The shape I would give it, per profile:

- Depth sets the floor, as today. Time lifts the floor toward the profile's maximum. Speed is the depth speed, plus hold time over a `rampMs` value applied to the gap up to the maximum.
- `rampMs` of 0 means off, which is exactly today's behaviour, so defaults do not move until we tune them.
- The hold clock resets when the pointer leaves the zone or changes direction, so a correction never inherits the previous run's speed.

That keeps the prop surface as one object, `selectionAutoscroll`, with a `mouse` and a `touch` partial profile of six fields each, and acceleration is just one of them. I would tune a default of about 1500 ms for touch and 1000 ms for mouse, then let you feel it out.

Here is the full knob set, with what each maps to, and then the honest answer on `propsWithDefaults`.

**What is fixed today**

| concern | knob today | value | where |
|---|---|---|---|
| wheel gain | `wheelMultiplier` | 1 | Lenis, not exposed |
| wheel follow | `lerp` | 0.1 | Lenis, not exposed |
| touch gain | `touchMultiplier` | 1.3 | Lenis, not exposed |
| flick inertia | `touchInertiaMultiplier` | 30 | Lenis, not exposed |
| flick follow | `syncTouchLerp` | 0.1 | Lenis, not exposed |
| top speed | none | unbounded | does not exist yet |
| autoplay creep | `creepMsPerPx` | tuned | already a prop |
| selection autoscroll | two static profiles | tuned | statics only |

So "normal scroll acceleration" is really two things: the gain, how much each wheel notch or finger pixel adds, and the follow, how fast the transform chases its target. Neither has a cap, which is why a fast flick can outrun the padding. The cap is the one new mechanism; everything else is exposing what exists.

**The layout as JSON, one nested prop per concern**

```json
{
  "scroll": {
    "wheel": { "gain": 1,   "follow": 0.1, "maxPxPerMs": 0 },
    "touch": { "gain": 1.3, "follow": 0.1, "inertia": 30, "maxPxPerMs": 0 }
  },
  "selection": {
    "autoscroll": {
      "mouse": { "zonePx": 32, "restPx": 0,  "reachPx": 160, "minPxPerMs": 0.15, "maxPxPerMs": 2,   "rampMs": 0 },
      "touch": { "zonePx": 96, "restPx": 24, "reachPx": 0,   "minPxPerMs": 0.06, "maxPxPerMs": 0.9, "rampMs": 0 }
    }
  }
}
```

- `gain` is the acceleration factor you asked about. Wheel gain of 2 means each notch moves twice as far.
- `follow` is the lerp. Higher is snappier, lower glides longer. It is what a reader feels as acceleration and deceleration.
- `maxPxPerMs` caps the velocity, 0 means unbounded, which is today's behaviour. This is the "how fast it can go" knob and needs a clamp in the Lenis fork.
- `inertia` is the flick multiplier, touch only.
- `rampMs` is the hold-time acceleration for selection autoscroll from the previous message, 0 means off.

An author writes only the leaf they care about and everything else stays tuned:

```ts
<VirtualScroller :scroll="{ wheel: { gain: 1.6 } }" />
```

**Is structuredClone enough?** For what `propsWithDefaults` does, yes. For nested extension, no, and no cloner could be. The reason is Vue, not the cloner: a prop's default factory only runs when the prop is absent. Pass `{ wheel: { gain: 1.6 } }` and Vue hands the class exactly that object, the default is never consulted, and the touch branch is simply missing. Cloning protects the default from being shared between instances. Merging a partial over it is a different job.

That job belongs on the class as a plain getter, which keeps it leaf-tracked and costs nothing:

```ts
get scrollKnobs() {
  return this.self.mergeKnobs(this.self.SCROLL_DEFAULTS, this.props.scroll);
}
```

with `mergeKnobs` a static deep merge for plain objects, and the defaults living as statics, where the two selection profiles already live. The `propsDefaults` entry for `scroll` becomes `{}` rather than the full tree, so the type says "partial of the knob shape" and the getter says "full shape". I would not teach `propsWithDefaults` to merge, since a merged prop would read differently from every other prop in Vue and the class getter already gives the right result with one line.

Yes, and it falls out of two things that were already there. The defaults are a value on the class, and a hosted capability owns its own tuning as statics. So the host's defaults are just the capabilities' statics assembled into a tree, and a page overrides any leaf of that tree without knowing which class owns it.

The composition runs in both directions:

- **Reuse.** A different host can pick up the same profile. A text editor's drag-to-select can take `VirtualScrollerSelection.Class.AUTOSCROLL_MOUSE` as its default, and a chat list can take the touch one. One tuned cadence, owned in one place, reused by name.
- **Override at the owner.** Because the host reads `VirtualScrollerSelection.Class`, a subclass of the selection with a re-tuned profile changes every scroller's default in one line, with no scroller code touched. And a subclass of the scroller can re-tune a leaf with `...super.propsDefaults` and a deeper spread, while the page keeps its per-instance override on top.

So there are three layers that all read as one object at runtime: the capability's static, the host's defaults, the page's partial prop. Each layer is a plain value, each is testable with nothing mounted, and `nestedProps` is the only mechanism.

One thing worth noting for the standard later: this only works because a `$`-cached static getter is not used for these profiles. A plain static getter returns a fresh object per read, so two hosts filling from the same profile never share a mutable object. A cached one would have been filled in place by the first host and leaked into the second. That is the same trap as the shared-registry fork, in the other direction, and probably deserves a sentence in the caches guide when this ships.
